title: Date published: May 24, 2026 The Silent, Inconspicuous Disappearance of Howlers
author: Rocchi, Francesco
summary: A high school History and Literature teacher describes a quiet but meaningful shift he has noticed in his students' work after implementing sustained spaced retrieval practice: the near-disappearance of 'howlers' — those spectacular, egregious student errors that suggest complete disconnection from the material. Rocchi frames the observation carefully, acknowledging that his struggling students still struggle and his strongest students would have succeeded regardless. What has changed is the baseline: misconceptions are being caught and corrected before assessments rather than surfacing as unguided guesses. The mechanism Rocchi attributes this to is the retrieval cycle itself. Through multiple rounds of retrieval, explanation, summarization, and reflection, students — even distracted or disengaged ones — have encountered the material enough times to form some actual connection with it. They are no longer forced to concoct answers from the first concept that surfaced during a lesson. The article's deeper claim is about the root cause of howlers: they are a feedback failure. When teachers do not check for comprehension in a timely manner, misconceptions embed themselves in student memory and persist. Spaced retrieval practice functions as a continuous error-correction mechanism that removes the conditions under which howlers form. Rocchi's note is modest — 'it isn't flashy or apparent' — but his argument is that this invisible baseline lift is real, worth noticing, and entirely attributable to sustained formative practice.
points: Howlers — the most egregious student errors — arise not from laziness but from feedback failure: when students face assessments without timely checks for comprehension, misconceptions accumulate and produce the catastrophic guesses that appear in classwork.

Spaced retrieval practice changes the baseline for struggling students not by converting them into strong students but by ensuring they have cycled through the material enough times to avoid total disconnection — a modest but measurable and real outcome.

The disappearance of howlers is a signal worth tracking precisely because it is invisible; teachers looking only for dramatic improvement in grades miss the quieter evidence that comprehension is being built at the floor.
quotes: As every teacher knows, or experiences sooner or later, students can make mistakes so huge you start thinking they're making it on purpose—for some obscure reason. There are loads of funny stories and anecdotes any teacher can tell.

I think that this kind of mistakes is getting rarer among my students because they are not resorting to mere guessing anymore. Nor do they concoct answers using the first concepts they catch on the fly during lessons.

For once, I think I could take credit for this: through sustained, spaced retrieval practice, it can hardly happen that students have to face assessment without having any clue of what is expected of them. As distracted, uninterested or simply struggling as they may be, they nonetheless undergo several cycles of retrieval, explanation, summarization, exposition and reflection.

As I was saying, it isn't flashy or apparent, but it does provide a boost—subtle, yet important—to the general activity of the classroom. Something is moving, and if you listen carefully enough, you can perceive the shift.

Ultimately, what causes the most egregious howlers is the lack of feedback: when the teacher doesn't check for comprehension in a timely manner, all sorts of mistakes are smuggled into classwork—and into the heads of the students, where they stick tenaciously.
